A 1970 book by Ivan Illich argues that these institutions encourage their members to confuse process for substance. A. S. Neill founded a radical English one named Summerhill, which helped inspire John Holt to found the movement encouraging people to find alternatives to these institutions. This concept's two main divisions are realis and irrealis, the former of which includes the "energetic" one. One book with this concept in its title describes this concept as "not a biologically driven complex" and begins with the observation that "no man sees the world through pristine eyes." Time inconsistency models characterize how this process is conducted by an individual at different points in time. Preference relations dictate this process's outcome. Name this process that lends its name to fields of economics studying people's systematic actions among a set of alternatives.

This thinker argued that language, religion, and division of labor held human communities together. This man's normative theory envisioned a future in which people would "live for others." In an experiment by Watanabe et al., these animals could be trained to tell apart Picasso and Monet paintings, and Herbranson and Schroeder found that these animals were not fooled by the Monty Hall problem. Nancy Frishberg argued that these constructs reject the Steady State theory since they have become less iconic and more arbitrary over time.
